paragraphs.text: The Independent Fragments from the Catena on the Prophets

For the righteous man is not in youth, since "having been made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled long years." The words "Do not say, 'I am too young'" are addressed to one who does not walk in blameworthy ways. Rehoboam was such a young man: he "forsook the counsel of the elders" and followed that of the young men, and so he did not keep the kingdom as he had received it.

The cauldron that is set boiling is fired from the face of the north, for the north is at once enemy and avenger. That is why the one who has sinned is handed over. If he sinned by blasphemy, he "is handed over to Satan, so that he may be taught not to blaspheme"; if by fornication, he is handed over "to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord." And whom does it set burning? Those who dwell on the earth, not those who sojourn on it. For he shoots "flaming arrows" at those who do not guard their own hearts with all vigilance, so that any sin whatever sets them ablaze.

He speaks of a lion, a wolf and a leopard as those who strike them. It seems that attacks on our conduct come from those figuratively called lions, while attacks on our knowledge come from those who want to harm the soul's power of insight. For the leopard is said to spring above all at the eyes, while the lion, as we are told, haunts the cities when it grows old, wanting to hunt men. It is also said that fire comes out of its bones when they are struck or crushed. Perhaps Nebuchadnezzar could be both lion and leopard. He took the city and, like a leopard, plucked out its eyes, the king along with the leading men, and later he also put out Zedekiah's eyes. His bones could be understood as Nebuzaradan, who burned the city.

He teaches us to examine carefully what the passage about sacrifices means, and the oracles give us starting points when they say: "A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit," and "Offer a sacrifice of righteousness." Those who were not so disposed, but were excited about bodily sacrifices, the Savior turned around, saying: "If you had known what this means, 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice,' you would not have condemned the guiltless." Paul taught that such legislation concerns mystical things when he said: "who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things."

The turtledove and the swallow, the birds of the field, are the intelligent hearers and those able to speak the better things. They kept the proper time for their comings, so that what is said reaches the hearers, the swallow's coming coinciding with the turtledove's.

Aquila and Theodotion rendered: "For he who formed all things is he, and Israel is the rod of his inheritance." Now if Israel is the rod of his inheritance, and he has also received the nations as an inheritance, according to "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance," then the nations too will be Israel.

God is just in not listening to those who did not listen to him. And it is just that the demons will not be able to save those who burned incense to them when the time of evils comes. So when God does not listen, it is a terrible thing to seek help from demons. Instead we must cling to God. He has turned away because of our sins, but he does not disregard those who take refuge in him earnestly and with perseverance.
He did not say, "I will not hear you," but "them." He shows that even then, if they repent and you ask on their behalf, I will hear.

He called abandonment an action, for God is said to destroy when he takes away his own tent. Alternatively, a destruction by his hand that is worthy of God is the change from vice to virtue, according to "I will bring my hands upon you, and I will refine you with fire until you are pure," when the defilements that sin left in us are destroyed. "I will scatter them" is of the same kind. Since they joined together in impiety toward me, I will break up their most wicked gathering and agreement, just as he divided the tongues of the tower-builders and kept their united impiety from growing. And "they have been made childless, they have destroyed my people" is an accusation against the rulers and the priests. These stood in the place of fathers to the peoples, yet they became bereft of their children by sowing impiety instead of pious teaching. Perhaps it is not even possible to destroy a people without first making one's own soul childless of the offspring of virtue, for no one who is good destroys another.

The souls of the ungodly would be widows, having lost Christ the bridegroom. When they perish, their mothers too are in misery: those who "begot them in Christ" and "were in labor until Christ was formed in them," and who after milk raised them on solid food until they were young men. The multitude of widows is not like "the stars of heaven" but like the sand of the sea. In the literal sense, when very many fell in war the women became widows and the mothers were in misery.

He commands us not to carry a burden of sins, nor to have to say, "Like a heavy load they have weighed upon me." Then we may become kings and rulers, sitting firmly on the throne of David, which is the church of Christ, so that it may be said of us: "You set on their head a crown of precious stone." Such people have also mounted chariots and horses, for they bridle the body and hold back its irrational impulses. And so the city will be inhabited forever, and because of the virtue of its leaders and the excellent way of life of its inhabitants, people will come from every side bringing gifts. They will come from the cities of Judah, of Those Who Confess to God; from those around Jerusalem, the Vision of peace; from the land of Benjamin, the Son of the plain, a land with no "height raised up against the knowledge of God"; from the mountain, which is the gospel word; and from the south country, which stands opposed to the wind that blows from the north. These will bring a sacrifice "holy and pleasing to God," the dedication of the soul. They will also bring rational whole burnt offerings, burning up through the Spirit all the matter that is liable to the eternal fire. Their "prayer is as incense, and the lifting up of their hands an evening sacrifice." They also offer frankincense, whose name means Whitening, casting off every gloomy disposition, so that the words "Who is this who comes up made white?" fit them. In this way they will be able to bring praise into the house of the Lord, "having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing" that might cling to the church of Christ. But if we do nothing of the kind, we shall suffer what the threat that follows announces.

The apostle showed what the house built with righteousness is when he said: "You are God's field, God's building." He also says: "No one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds on it," and so on. So through the one who taught him, the believer has Christ Jesus as his foundation. Someone may build on it well, with "gold," the doctrines of truth, "silver," the saving word, and "precious stones," a building made of virtues. But if he builds badly and puts wicked things on Jesus, I mean "wood, hay, straw," how is he not impious? The woe comes upon him: "he who builds his house without righteousness." Whoever makes a lofty building that is not according to the word of God and the truth does not make his upper rooms with judgment. Understand those who teach either the truth or "knowledge falsely so called" in the same way. Paul, for example, builds the house, the church, with righteousness, and he builds Timothy, Luke and others like them as upper rooms with judgment.

Following on from what came before, you might say that this is also said about the false teachers. As Solomon says: "He who gathers treasures by a lying tongue pursues vain things and will come into the snare of death." Such people build houses for themselves in the name of a church, but it is the church "of evildoers." To them it is said with irony: "You have built yourself a well-proportioned house, airy upper rooms"; in these they thought they had built refreshment. Through the windows you think you have lit your buildings with the light of knowledge and used wood that does not rot to build the house, and you paint it with vermilion in imitation of the blood of Christ. But you will not reign, even if you were provoked in the cedar of your father. The cedar is the sinner's father: a lofty tree, arrogant and hostile, the devil or the ruler of wicked words. Those who have built such things will perish of famine, for they will neither eat nor drink. Nor did they know righteousness, since they did not know Christ; for to do what is just, he says, is the mark of those who know God. In those who are not such, the eyes are not good, since they do not see the truth, and neither is the heart, which is full of false doctrines. Through these they lead others astray and murder their souls, shedding innocent blood with a lying and deceitful tongue. And this is worse than slaughter by the sword.

Jeremiah calls this Jehoiakim Jeconiah. His father was called Eliakim, and Pharaoh Neco renamed him Jehoiakim. The Babylonian killed the father and threw his body out before the gate, as the present prophet says, and Josephus too in the tenth book of the Antiquities. For "signet" the Others rendered "seal." Whoever recovers through repentance what is according to the image becomes a seal, or signet ring, on God's right hand. For God's right hand is understood as good works, since he sets the sheep "on the right." This is the seal the father gave to the prodigal son when he returned. If Jeconiah had become this, he would have been a model of piety for his subjects, but he did not. Still, he did seem to obey the prophet who said, "Whoever goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who are besieging you will live"; for he went out with his mother and the nobles and deserted to the Babylonians. Even if, he says, he had shown complete repentance, so as to become "a seal of the righteousness of circumcision," as the divine apostle puts it, and in that respect to seem to be on God's right hand, he would surely still have been handed over to pay the penalty for his former sins, though a lighter one. For after he had been chastened in Babylon in prison and in chains, under Evil-merodach he was restored to ease and became the king's table companion, and so he ended his life in a foreign land.

What he forbids is not simply listening to a prophet, but listening to words of prophets uttered in imitation. For whoever listens to a prophet such as Moses listens not to him but to the Lord who speaks through him. The false prophets, however, make people vain: by not making the hearer turn back they make him vain, since they speak a vision of their own heart. For a mind that tackles things without God's help speaks a vision of the heart, not from the mouth of the one who grants speech and gives light. Sometimes, though, the vision of the heart and the word of the Lord's mouth coincide. That is why he does not simply censure the vision of the heart, but only when the other is absent. They coincide in the one who says: "I pray with the mouth, and I pray also with the mind."

He prophesies about an earthquake and about the wrath of the Lord going out against the ungodly. "The anger has not turned back": not without qualification, but "until he has done it," since he turns back once he has done it. What "the word of the Lord" did not do, the anger of the Lord does. David says what the anger of the Lord does in "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger." So he does not stop rebuking until he has accomplished the purpose for which he rebukes, just as the wrath does not stop until it has disciplined completely. And he will not only do it but also establish and confirm it. "From the purpose of his heart" is a riddle that, he says, will be understood at the last, namely, what has been said about anger and wrath. Thanks, then, to the one who has revealed to us what was hidden until now.

Therefore they did not escape my notice when they drove my people into wickedness. For he who lets even a prophet know what happens everywhere knows it much better himself. "The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world," and "in him we live and move and have our being," as Paul said to the Athenians. "Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord?" is of the same kind, for by his power he is near to all. So prayers are not offered to God as though he were far away. Of the Son too it is said: "He was in the world, and the world came into being through him." For it is he who says, "I am a God who is near." He also said: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there among them," and he also says: "Behold, I am with you always, until the end of the age."

Our soul leaves no part of the body empty of it: wherever there is sensation, there the soul is, and it reaches the whole body. In the same way nothing is empty of God. And yet, though he fills all things, he does not fill the sinner, because the sinner is filled with unclean spirits. Such a person cannot be filled by God unless he is rid of the others that fill him. For God fills those who are worthy, in heaven and on earth. It does not say "the earth and everything in it is the Lord's," but "the earth and its fullness," as though there were some in it who are not the fullness of the earth. The fullness of the earth is those who are filled by the one who said: "Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord."

The false prophets also misused "Thus says the Lord," passing themselves off as true prophets, so there was a need for signs to tell the two apart. According to the apostle, there was the gift of discernment of spirits, and whoever had it discerned the spirits, both the divine and the evil, just as a money-changer tells genuine coin from counterfeit. But even without that general skill, what is said here is enough to tell them apart. My word, he says, is not empty, fit only as food for irrational animals, but is like wheat, food for rational beings.

He said, "What is the chaff to the wheat?" and not "to the barley." For the Lord set out loaves, barley ones for the less rational and wheat ones for the rational. That is why here too he did not say "What is the chaff to the barley?" but "to the wheat," pointing precisely to rational food. There is also another sign: the words of the Lord are like an axe that splits rock. When the hearer who is rebuked burns, so that he says, "Was not my heart burning within me?", the word is fire and wheat. But if he is delighted, listening to things meant to please, it is chaff. The word of God is also an axe, able to split not only wood but rock as well. This is not the rock [?] understood as Christ, but the opposing rock, which must be cut, according to "Rocks will be shattered before the Lord."

Suppose someone buys a garment from its rightful owner: he holds it lawfully, while one who stole it has it, but not justly. In the same way, among those who teach from Scripture, those who carry its words with a spurious and counterfeit soul are stealing them. Of them it might be said: "All who came before me are thieves and robbers, and the sheep did not listen to them." Such a person uses the gospel word without being disposed toward it in faith or living by it, and proclaims the word with an alien purpose. He is a thief, and it will be said to him: "You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?"

What the whole world is, man alone is by a certain analogy. You will find that one person is called heaven, when he bears "the image of the heavenly," and another earth, if he has "the image of the earthly" (for it was said to the one who sinned, "You are earth"). Another has rivers within him "springing up to eternal life," if he has most refreshing words [?] "which God formed to sport in it." And in particular you will find one called sun, another moon, and others stars, since "so it is with the resurrection of the dead."
And a little later:

But now the parable says that he is a very bad fig. Virtue sweetens a person as he ripens, so that his whole soul, spirit and body become sweet, because the quality that comes from virtues has been placed in him. Wickedness, on the other hand, makes him bad and inedible. If someone looks for figs that are not very good, he looks for them outside the mysteries of godliness and the temple of God, and the same goes for those that are not very bad. For if one comes to discipleship itself, the figs before the temple of the Lord are either very good (such as Christ knows how to make) or bad; for not even the bad fig outside has thrown the words of God behind it. So two baskets lie around the temple of God and the divine doctrines. And the one who chooses knows how to place each. He will not allow the quality of a bad fig to be mixed with the very good ones (for "a little leaven leavens the whole lump"), nor the reverse. Perhaps the basket of bad figs is the Gehenna of eternal fire, and the basket of good ones the kingdom of heaven.
And a little later:

But when did the prophet see the baskets? After the captivity, he says. If you look at the coming of the Savior and the captivity of the people, and at us, who are foreigners by nature and outside Jerusalem but are now becoming good figs through faith in God and the sweetness of the truth, you will see the basket of good figs. But if you look at those of the circumcision after this captivity, you will see the basket of bad and inedible figs. Yet it is not enough for the figs to be very good; they must also be like the early figs. For the one who is being saved is never compared to a late fig.

Christ is builder and master builder, of whom it was said in the prophets: "He will build my city and bring back the captivity of my people." So the Lord says: "I will build, and I will not pull down." For though God is good, he does pull down certain buildings. The building of unclean spirits within us must be torn down, and then a temple built for God out of virtues and right doctrines, so that his glory may also be seen in it. He is also a farmer who plants and grafts in those who are worthy. The Savior, as the root that holds up all the branches, says: "I am the true vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the farmer. Every branch that remains in me and bears good fruit my Father prunes, so that it may bear more fruit; but every branch that remains in me and does not bear fruit my Father cuts off and throws into the fire." The branch that "remains in him and does not bear fruit" is found not among the gentiles but among believers. Such is the one who says he is a believer yet sins without fear; he is rightly cut off. But he prunes the branch that bears fruit, so that if, being human, it overlooks something, it may correct it.
As we were saying, the Seventy placed this one first among the visions against the nations, while the Others did the opposite. Elam is an Arabian nation lying by the Red Sea.

They prided themselves on their archery, never having learned to sing: "For I will not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me." He threatens to stir up nations against him from every side, and so he summons winds from the regions they set out from. Each of us, depending on his condition, bears the same name as an Elamite, an Idumean, a Moabite, an Egyptian or an Israelite. And it is possible to change from one nation into another, for better or worse, since the nations of the soul can pass into one another. Yet each of us, according to what he has stored up, will drink the cup of the Lord's wrath, either undiluted or mixed; for we have all sinned, some more and some less. Just as Israel was named for what he did, when he prevailed with God in the wrestling, so some are Elamites, that is, Cast Aside and Blameworthy, for that is what the name means. They are cast aside [?], then, "to dishonorable passions." Paul also shows which winds the passage means, when he says: "so that we may no longer be tossed by the waves and carried about by every wind of teaching, by human cunning, in the scheming of error." The one who is Cast Aside is carried about by every wind, whether of teaching, of anger or of desire. There are four general winds that trouble the human soul: desire, fear, pleasure and grief, and the Elamite who is abandoned by God is handed over to them. But what the bow of Elam is, in which lies the beginning of its dominion, David himself said in song: "Behold, the sinners bent the bow, they made ready arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the moonless dark at the upright in heart."

But when the Savior came, he brought the four winds upon the Elamites who surround us, in order to scatter them. For hostile powers are handed over to other hostile powers to be punished, as Pharaoh was to Nebuchadnezzar. If you shut venomous snakes up together, hunger makes the stronger eat the weaker, until the strongest of all, filled with the snakes it has devoured, becomes what is called a basilisk, whose venom withers a fruit-bearing tree by its mere glance. In the same way the evil powers are punished by one another, until at last only "the last enemy" of Christ, death, is left. This is the basilisk of which it says: "You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk." For Christ, being stronger than the basilisk, has trodden on it and has given us "authority to tread on snakes and scorpions."

There is a Babylonian man and there is a Babylonian infant, and we must fight against both, that is, against passions that are either full-grown or only now beginning. But "blessed is the one who seizes the infants of Babylon and dashes them against the rock" (that is, Christ) before they grow up into men. Still more blessed is it to wipe out the Babylonian seed, meaning a thought of Confusion. (The opposite of this is the seed of which it is said, "Blessed is the one who has seed in Zion," and "Blessed are those who sow beside every water, where ox and donkey tread.") Not only a man or a child, then, but even a mere seed, for a seed can bear fruit if it is cultivated. And what is the water beside which the good seed must be sown? The washing of regeneration. There "ox and donkey tread": the ox is the clean one, the Israelite; the donkey is the one unclean by birth, the gentile. These animals are symbols of the word announced to the Israelites and the word preached to the gentiles.

The Babylonian holds a sickle not to save but to cut down and reap the [?] holy church. Let us destroy him before we suffer this, by wiping out the arguments of the heretics. Paul was such a one when he said, "being ready to punish every disobedience," and "casting down every height raised up against the knowledge of God." Then he testifies to the power of Greek reasoning, that all the nations yield to it because it seems somehow to offer proof.

He says "sheep" as of a single one that has gone astray. In the Gospel too he says, "The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost." And in the parable only one of the hundred was lost, the one the shepherd who came among us came to find; he took it up on his shoulders and restored it to the number of the ninety-nine. For we are all one body and one sheep: one is a foot, another a head, another something else, and the shepherd came and brought together "bone to bone and joint to joint," and having united it he carried it up to his own country. This unity comes about through love and truth and good choice. By his own word, then, he united all. But if some showed themselves disobedient, they acquired an incurable affliction. So the whole Israelite people is one according to true kinship, "for we are all one body and one bread, and we partake of the one Spirit." The wandering sheep is the one who fails in the pursuit of what is fitting in word and deed, either by not seeking or by not finding. The one who knows and does the things of true knowledge does not wander, but the one who wanders is driven off by lions. For "our adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour." And already "lion cubs, roaring to seize their prey and seeking their food from God," lie in wait for the righteous, wanting to drive us from the mountains of peace. But just as David seized the lion by its beard and strangled it, so let us ask the spiritual David, Christ, to seize the lion and destroy the whole council of the beasts. Here he takes two lions as types, the Assyrian and the Babylonian. According to the history in 2 Kings there are two: the Assyrian deported the sons of Israel "to Assyria to this day," and the Babylonian deported the sons of Judah "to Babylon." Yet here he did not say "first and second" but "first and last." For the first lion is the devil, our adversary, the "murderer" himself; the last, at the end of the age, is "the man of sin, the son of destruction, who exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship."

Israel cannot be restored to its pasture unless the two kings suffer what they must suffer in vengeance for those who were wronged. But do not take the passage simply of the devil or the antichrist; rather, let him be destroyed in me, "Satan being crushed under my feet shortly." When he destroys these two and those in between, he will restore Israel to its pasture; then it will graze on Carmel and in Bashan, on Mount Ephraim and in Gilead. Though there are so many places in Judea and in the [?] land being inherited, he named only these.

He calls Babylon a hammer, because by its own greed it pounded to pieces those on earth. When Solomon was building the divine temple, 1 Kings says in its praise that "no hammer or axe was heard in the house of God." The house is the church of God, in which no hammer should be heard. The hammer of the whole earth is the devil, and the one who pays it no heed is like some material that is struck by it and yet suffers nothing. For it says, "Behold, a man standing on a wall of adamant, and in his hand adamant"; and adamant is shattered by no hammer. So even if the devil, the hammer, stands over him, and the dragon lies beneath "like an anvil that cannot be beaten," the adamant that is in the Lord's hand and under his shelter will suffer nothing. For the saint is a wall of adamant, and remaining in the Lord's hands he is unharmed, even if caught between the hammer and the dragon. The more he is struck, the more brilliantly he displays his virtue. For the devil, like someone ignorant of the nature of stones, tests the adamant-like man with many blows, while God alone truly knows their nature. If there were no hammer, there would be no "beaten trumpet" of the law, which rouses people to the feasts of God or stirs those who hear it to war. Through varied temptations the hammer made Paul into such a trumpet: he suffered nothing from it, but with a loud voice he roused others to war against wickedness. So the hammer works the temptation, and the one descended from Cain serves the hammer, "a hammerer, a smith of bronze and iron." Such, in the Savior's case, were Judas and those who shouted "Crucify, crucify him": through such people they served the hammer.

The apostle too knows of vessels of wrath "prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy." For he divided all people into these two kinds of vessels, some of wrath, others of mercy: the one kind like Pharaoh and the Egyptians, the other like Paul and those who believed. But what is the Lord's treasury in which the vessels of wrath are kept? Perhaps the church, in which such people often lie hidden. There will come a time when he opens the church. For now it is shut, and the vessels of wrath graze together with the vessels of mercy, the chaff lies with the wheat, and in one net are both the fish to be thrown away and the choice ones. The Lord opens his treasury at the time of judgment, when the vessels of wrath are cast out and the one who is a vessel of mercy might fittingly say, "They went out from us, for they were not of us." But vessels that sin outside the treasury are not yet vessels of wrath but something lesser, for they are "servants who do not know their master's will and do not do it." They are therefore simply vessels kept for other uses.

Some of the captives of Judea, he says, will come bringing the good news of the vengeance on Babylon. He could also be speaking of those who turn back from idolatry, which he calls Babylon: they come to Zion, the Watchtower, that is, the church, and proclaim the vengeance that comes from the Lord our God.

Those in Babylon are many, those in Jerusalem very few. For it is said, "It was not because you were most numerous that the Lord your God loved you; for you are the fewest of all the nations." For truly "few are those who are saved and enter through the narrow gate." And everyone who draws a bow against "broad and spacious" Babylon is commanded to spare none of it.

However many thoughts a person has that stand opposed to godliness, so many are the Babylonians; they must be destroyed, since they are sinners of the earth. Whoever has been cleansed of them comes to be in the city of God, who avenges Babylon's insolence; for Babylon thought it had prevailed by its own power, and it boasted against God. When the temple had been burned, the sacred vessels were given to concubines for their use. Therefore he consumed the fruitless nation with fire, as if it were a thicket. That is why he says: "Behold, I am against you, insolent one, says the Lord of hosts."

He prophesies that the end will come all at once. For "just as in the days of the flood" and "in the days of Lot" everyone went about the business of life "until the flood and the fire came and took them all away," so the end will come suddenly. A symbol of this was Jericho, which fell all at once at the mere sound of trumpets. And at the time of the Savior's passion Babylon fell suddenly, when Christ abolished the doctrines about the idols of the gentiles and rescued those from among the gentiles who believed.

Nebuchadnezzar's cup is golden "for the deception of people," so that they take it and drink, looking at the gold and not reckoning the judgment it contains. For his wicked doctrines are adorned with fine diction, luring people with beauty of expression and technical method. Indeed every poet reputed to be supreme has fashioned a golden cup and put into it the poison of idolatry, of obscene speech, and of every evil of the soul. But Jesus took no thought for a golden cup, lest he should even seem to be like that one (that is why "we have this treasure in earthen vessels"); his care was for the salvation it holds. The golden cup, Babylon, when it comes to the vengeance, is in the hand of the Lord, the hand that once touched Job, and it makes the whole earth drunk with anger, with grief, with lusts, with vainglory (for there are as many kinds of drunkenness as there are sins), so that all are reeling as if from wine and have nothing firm. But the righteous person is not earth. Though he is on earth, he has "his citizenship in heaven," and he would not hear, "You are earth, and to earth you will return," but rather, as is fitting: You are heaven, and to heaven you will return, for you bear "the image of the heavenly," and you stand firm.

If Babylon has not been despaired of (for otherwise he would not say, "if perhaps she will be healed"), what other soul shall we despair of? But if she has not been saved, that came about through her own fault, so that the best physicians can defend themselves and say: We treated Babylon, and she was not healed; let us abandon her. For it is not because of them, nor because of [?] the physicians, nor because of the balm, that she is not cured. The physicians are angels, who serve under the great physician, God, and wish to heal those who obey. If not, they will say: Let us abandon her, and let each of us go to his own place and his own work, for her judgment has drawn near to heaven. So they condemn her as incurable and as about to suffer what befits those who are past hope. For physicians of bodies too abandon the incurable, lest they die in their hands; and this is what the angels do. The more we sin, the more our judgment grows, and it rises up as far as the stars, that is, the saints. And then God brings forth his own judgment to humble the judgment that sin has raised so high, humbling the sin and repaying according to desert.

Isaiah too prophesied: "On a level mountain raise a signal, lift up your voice to them; summon them with your hand." The prophets were urging the Persians and Medes, since they were about to conquer Babylon, to raise the signal for battle against her walls as she was about to be taken; by this signal they show the soldiers it is time to attack. He also urges them to have their weapons ready; he means the bows of the Medes.

In agreement with "every man has become foolish, without knowledge," Paul says, "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?" The time of visitation is above all the overthrow of idolatry that followed the coming of Christ. The weapons of war that the Babylonian scattered are the men of Israel and Judah who were skilled in war; on account of them he threatens to spare no one.

The riders of horses are the demons who sit astride fleshly pleasures. For long ago, in Egypt, "he threw horse and rider into the sea." These demons yoke together in us various passions opposed to the four virtues and so build chariots. The one who is hot-tempered and strong for wickedness is a man; the one dissolved in pleasures is a woman; an old man is one "grown old in evil days"; young men are those of whom Isaiah says, "The young shall hunger, and youths shall grow weary, and the chosen shall be without strength," and the opposite: "But those who wait for God shall renew their strength; they shall grow wings like eagles; they shall run and not grow weary." Here he speaks of those chosen in wickedness, as in "and his food is choice"; and those who are chosen for virtue are swallowed up by Nebuchadnezzar. He also had virgins: some Vestals, some Pythian priestesses, and others besides. And a soul that has not received the divine seed is a virgin for him. He also has shepherds who instruct their followers in bad teaching, and farmers who sow "the weeds" and cultivate "thorns and thistles," that is, the worldly cares of human beings. He also has governors and rulers in wickedness, and above all those "against whom our struggle is, against the principalities, against the powers." To all these, then, God pays back their due in the sight of those who have just said, "Come, let us declare in Zion the mighty works of God."

He calls Babylon a mountain because of the loftiness of its kingdom, a kingdom corrupted by idolatry and by the unjust deeds through which it corrupted others. The city was also on high ground because of the river beside it, from which flights of steps led up to the city. It was in two parts, lying along the river on either bank, and in addition the city's walls were extremely high. The hand is the punishing power, which brings her down from her own security and guard as if from rocks, and destroys even her stones with fire, making them useless, so that no stone is left fit for solid building. In the anagogical sense the devil too is called a mountain, as in Zechariah: "Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel?" And concerning the one who had a "deaf and dumb" demon the Savior said, "If you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, 'Move,' and it will move." The devil, then, is a mountain, corrupted by his own wickedness and corrupting all who set their minds on earthly things.

"Sanctify nations" stands for "set them apart." For sanctification is service to God, even when it is service in punishment and the one set apart for it is profane. Such was Cyrus, to whom he says through Isaiah, "But you did not know me." He called some of those who marched against Babylon "nations," and among them he calls the Armenians "Ararat."

The earth was shaken: its inhabitants had in former times been firmly settled and secure in the dominions and kingdoms they held, but now they were receiving desolation, an evil and painful change. And every mind that has held Babylonian land, shaken out of its attachment to such impiety and Confusion, casts off that disposition in order to take up a spiritual and heavenly state.

For it was God who did this, he who also said through Isaiah to Cyrus, "I will go before you and level the mountains; I will shatter doors of bronze and crush bars of iron." Outside writers too record that Babylon had such gates, and that it was captured by way of the descents into the river that ran through its middle, the two parts being joined by bridges at the ascents leading up to the city, since the city was divided into two parts. And the history says that while those at the far edges of the city were being captured, the rest, who were celebrating a festival, did not notice because of the city's size, even though, as is likely, the city was full of uproar, with some running to bring the news and others returning from bringing it. By "compacts" he seems here to mean the houses, for they stood joined to one another in continuous rows. That is why he adds, "the houses of the king of Babylon," and what follows; that is, the fortresses formed from the buildings standing together in them.

For "they will tip him over and crush his vessels," Symmachus said, "and they will drain him and empty his vessels." For he kept to the figure of wine, showing that he will be emptied of good things. Prosperity, then, is not good for the boastful, just as it was not for the rich man in Hades, who was punished because of it. The word "mixtures," used as of wine, Aquila rendered "horns," which was an ancient kind of cup (for people drank from horns), and that is why the expression "to mix" has remained in use. The vessels, then, are the cities, and their contents are the people and the wealth; for they carried off the one and burned the other. Calamity puts to shame the hopes placed in demons; but "hope" in God "does not put to shame." It was at Bethel in Samaria that Jeroboam set up the heifers. The one who claims to be strong is not saved, for "a king is not saved by great power." The day of Moab is the time of punishment, and "evil" means the hardships that will overtake him. He calls on all those around to set upon him; that is what "stir" means, namely to shame and grief, "for God opposes the proud."
"Epicheirion" denotes either the scepter, or those under his rule, or hired men; for "epicheira" means wages.

He will clap his hands, the hands with which he used to clap, gloating over Israel and acting insolently against God. Those who "trusted in the fortifications" of their cities abandoned them and lived in the rocks beside the ravines, imitating doves in wantonness and in folly. For doves sometimes nest in places from which anyone who wishes can easily take their young. Wanton is the one initiated into the rites of Baal-Peor, and foolish the one devoted to useless and vain idols; Moab was such a one. For "the fool said in his heart, 'There is no God,'" either being altogether godless or reckoning that the God who truly exists does not exist at all.

Jerusalem, as has often been said, is understood as the church, which is the city of God built of living stones. From it the sinner is cast out and handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, that is, to Satan. For Paul says of the fornicator, "to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord"; and in 1 Timothy, of the blasphemers, "whom I handed over to Satan, so that they may be taught not to blaspheme." Let the one cast out of Jerusalem know that unless he spends a sufficient time outside the church doing what he ought, he will not return to Jerusalem. A person who sins is cast out even if he has not been cast out by men. Once outside, he must not neglect to build a house and plant gardens. For if he does not do these things and does not complete the symbolic number of "the seventy years," which is a number of sabbath and rest, he will not return to share in the communion of the church, but remains condemned outside. [?] ... the one who said of wisdom, "Her I sought to take as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty." One must love her, as Solomon taught in Proverbs when he said, "Love her, and she will guard you," and "Fortify her, and she will exalt you." And understand the other virtues as wives besides wisdom. For in this way it will be permitted to take many wives, and from them one must beget children: from wisdom a word of wisdom, so that you may build up others too; from temperance works of temperance, so that you may make people temperate in life and in word; from justice works of justice in partnerships and dealings. And by teaching people to be just you will beget children from justice, producing sons and, from the sons, daughters [?]: the sons are the divine thoughts and doctrines, the daughters the actions.

When Jerusalem was in turmoil with the Babylonian pressing upon it, people naturally took refuge in foreknowledge, wanting to know what would happen. The false prophets insisted that they were foretelling by the Holy Spirit, while of the others some offered divinations and others dreams. That is why no impious foreknowledge of any kind should be tolerated; for if the stars really do act on us, we pray in vain. Therefore he says, "Let the astrologers of heaven tell what the Lord plans concerning you," and "There shall be no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel." Become worthy, then, of divine foreknowledge. For after "there shall be no divination in Israel" he adds, "In due time it will be told to Jacob and to Israel what God will accomplish."

Every elder who does such things will suffer such things at the hands of the king of Babylon. For if one who partakes of the Eucharist unworthily receives it to his judgment, how much more the one who sits in the presbytery with a defiled conscience and pollutes the council of Christ? For what devout person sitting with him will dare to say, "I have not sat with the council of vanity," and what follows?
Jeremiah [?] 37:17–18.

You might say that he also displays his own goodness, and that it is because of this goodness that he brings severity upon those of hers who need it. Therefore, after she has been healed through pain, the city, he says, will be built upon its height. What height? "A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden"; such is the one who thinks nothing lowly or merely human, by which he means pleasures, wealth on earth, and petty glory. For "it has been raised with Christ and seeks the things above." When you do these things, "your city will be built upon its height."
He says this as of something rare.
It is Scripture's custom, after bitter words, to speak kind words for
From Origen's Letter to Africanus, on Susanna.

I remember talking about many things with a learned Hebrew who was reputed among them to be a wise man. From him, on the understanding that the story of Susanna is not rejected, I learned the names of the elders as well, as they appear in Jeremiah, in this form: "May the Lord make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire, because of the lawlessness they committed in Jerusalem" (Jer. 36:22–23).

I also know another Hebrew who passed on traditions like these about the same elders. The captives hoped that through the coming [?] of Christ they would be set free from slavery to the enemy, and these elders pretended to know and explain the things concerning Christ. Each of them would say, as if in secret, that God had granted him to beget the Christ. Then the woman, deceived by the hope of giving birth to the Christ, would give herself to the deceiver. In this way the elders Ahab and Zedekiah "committed adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens" (Jer. 36:23). That is why Daniel rightly called one of them "grown old in wicked days" (Sus. 52 LXX, Theodotion), while the other heard the words "This is how you used to treat the daughters of Israel," and what follows (Sus. 57 LXX, Theodotion). These, then, are the two elders who gave false testimony against Susanna.

consolation, and after kind words to speak more bitter ones again. This keeps people from despising "the riches of the kindness" of God and so storing up for themselves "wrath on the day of wrath." That is why he says: "If the wrath comes, it will not turn back until it has done what God wills." God wills, and wrath comes about so that what God wills may be done. If someone does not want to be within the will of God the Word, wrath is let loose upon him. So let us not need a wrath that disciplines, or anger.

They will not travel through the desert as before, but by the ordinary road through inhabited country. Figuratively, too, it says "in consolation," because "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted."

The far-off islands are those tossed by the waves of this life, which are far from the truth until they come to salvation. And God has redeemed Jacob, for "the yoke that lay on them has been taken away, and the rod on their neck," as Isaiah says. The passage also shows that he himself rescued us from the devil's power. For what could we have done against the one who said, among other things, "I will take the whole world in my hand like a nest"? To him we say through Christ: "Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O Hades, is your sting?"

Let the words "Let your voice cease from weeping" be spoken to those whose weeping makes them worthy of being called blessed. They are the ones who say in the Holy Spirit: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept when we remembered Zion."

It is written in Baruch as well: "Why is it that you are in the land of your enemies? You have been defiled along with the dead." When the righteous walk on it, it is a land of saints, but when many are sinners, it is a land of enemies. And so, he says, they will return in such a way that your children's return from the land of the enemies will be lasting, for those who have benefited from you and for your fruits. In Exodus, too, it is written that "God heard the people, their groaning because of their labors." That is like what is set down here, but here it is not about everyone. It is about Ephraim lamenting, and Ephraim is interpreted as "Fruitfulness."

God hears the sound of weeping from those who repent. But why did he speak of Ephraim lamenting over sins? First Kings shows why. Rehoboam ruled them harshly, and they ought to have endured it without revolting. Instead they cried out, "We have no portion in David," when Jeroboam, who was of the tribe of Ephraim, led the rebels. He made calves and turned the ten tribes away from the worship of God. Over these things they rightly lamented in repentance, and once the capture had disciplined them they cried out: "You disciplined me, Lord, and I was disciplined. Like a calf that has bolted from the herd, I strayed from your pasture, and I need your help. Unless you strengthen me, I am too weak to turn back. I ought to have repented before I was captured and obeyed your prophets, but I repented after the capture." He groans because he knows. How could someone groan without knowing that he sins, when he has done shameful things in his sins, and especially in his debauchery? "I repented so deeply that I could point you out to others." Ephraim's repentance was so great that God took up the words of confession from his mouth, and Ephraim heard the voice that said: "From my youth you are a beloved son, Ephraim."

A kind of Assyrian Nebuchadnezzar held all humanity captive, and Christ redeemed us from him. That is why Matthew, quoting Isaiah, says "to proclaim release to the captives"; Christ did not proclaim it to captives in the historical sense. He himself is also the righteous and holy mountain, for how could those words suit a lifeless thing? And if we are in him, in keeping with "and you in me," let us build on the righteous mountain. A person does this by coming to be in Judea, which is interpreted as "Confessing," when he confesses his sins to God and gives thanks; for "Tell your iniquities first, so that you may be justified." God has his cities, his buildings and his fields, as Paul also says: "You are God's field, God's building." Whoever has the mysteries and unspeakable doctrines of God built up within him is a temple of God and a holy of holies, and he is the capital city of all Judea.

The words "I will not reject Israel" seem to contradict what is said to them: "and the race of Israel will cease." Perhaps, then, the second was said about Israel according to the flesh. Also, the words about rejecting are not found in the other translators, but only in the Seventy. You may also understand it this way: for now I reject, but if it is exalted, I will not reject.

We are all in prison, especially when we are being tempted. That is when someone acquires a field, though without leaving the prison, and by God's will this acquisition belongs to those who contend well. The brothers: Hilkiah [?], for peace and portion are a matter of brothers [?]. The fruit of the portion of God is "Exaltation of God," for that is how Jeremiah is interpreted. And the fruit of peace is "Grace of God," for that is what Hanamel means. So the grace of God, being the offspring of peace, offers the prophet in prison his own field at God's command.

He draws up a deed of purchase. This is perhaps our understandings, memories and doctrines, through which we have acquired the field, that is, the labors of a godly life. Whoever is going to practice righteousness must first know about righteousness, and the same may be said of the other virtues. God takes care that the deed is placed in a vessel so that it will last longer. For "we have this treasure in earthen vessels," meaning either our own vessels or the plainness of Scripture's language. That is why "the ruler of this world was deceived": he despised the word of godliness because it was not in golden vessels adorned with fine diction and persuasive phrasing. And that is also why it lasted many days. For "my word and my preaching," says the one who holds the deed of purchase, "were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power." Having done what he was commanded, Jeremiah gives thanks to God. Notice how the prophet obeys before any advantage is visible. He adds that advantage afterward, when he foretells the recovery of the land. Prophecy acted out in deeds makes what is heard visible and the future as good as present, showing the whole in a part.

It is not plausible that the prophet, who was "sanctified from the womb" and full of the divine Spirit, would offer such great thanks for a plot bought for "seventeen shekels." But consider the sabbatical number seven, the symbol of rest, and the number ten, which is perfect and proper to God. Tithes are offered on the tenth day of the atonements, and the first giving of the law was the Ten Commandments. Then you will understand "the field": the one full of fruits fitting for saints. Such was the field of Jacob. When Isaac smelled it, he said: "See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field that the Lord has blessed." Such is the one who "has the fruits of the Spirit," so that he may "sow the things of the Spirit and reap eternal life." For he breathed out patience, kindness [?] … gives thanks, saying: "O Lord, you who are." For he looks to the one who truly is, "not looking at the things that are seen but at the things that are unseen."

Jeremiah recorded not only prophecies but also his own sufferings. Through the prophecies he teaches the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, and through the sufferings he gives examples of endurance. The false prophets suffered nothing of the kind, because they flattered. So in a time of persecution let us be ready to take our place with Jeremiah and with the apostle who said, "in prisons often." The words "the king could do nothing against them" showed that the king's own intention was more humane. An upright king should not let himself be carried along by the wicked people around him. Still, protection from those in power is often useful, and God often does good through it.

"I am afraid," he says, "that I may become a laughingstock to the deserters. That is what I take account of and worry about." Just as Jerusalem is handed over because of sins, so is the church. If someone like Hezekiah rules it, it is saved. But if someone like Zedekiah rules it, he saves it by being cut off from it and destroys it by staying. So if someone who defiles the church leaves it, he saves both the church and his own soul. But if, like Zedekiah, he delays his departure, "a little leaven leavens the whole lump."

Jeremiah tells him what the women will say as they are led away into exile: "Those who spoke peaceably to you, saying they would not hand you over to the Babylonian, have deceived you." They will stand together with [?] those who were the cause of his fall, for you will certainly be captured. Perhaps he is also blaming the false prophets, who promised peace in words. The prophet kindly hid the truth from the officials out of concern for the king. He did no harm by keeping silent about it now, since he had already read those words to them publicly.

When the prophet was given the choice of where he wanted to live, he passed over Babylon and chose Judea. He was avoiding the honor the king would give him, and he also chose it for the sake of the poor who had stayed behind to farm, so that he might look after the land for the poor and cultivate their souls with his prophecies. For the prophets divided the territory among themselves: Jeremiah took Judea, and Daniel and the three young men took Babylon.

A good man does not suspect anyone of being so wicked as to murder even those who have done no wrong. Why God allowed Gedaliah to be killed is a question for another discussion, and it belongs to the unsearchable judgments of God.

Connect the words "was it not the incense" with "the Lord remembered." It is clear that he is speaking of those who burn incense to idols, since the preceding words are added after they have admitted this. Still, let us ask whether someone who burns incense even to God, but not as he should, becomes a cause of the land's being made desolate. Suppose you offer physical incense as the Jews do. If you have virtue, you offer it well, because your inward fragrance is in harmony with it. But if you offer it with wickedness, you somehow taint even the outward fragrance and turn it into a stench. Then it could not be said that "the Lord smelled a pleasing odor," but the opposite. The pleasing odor before God was not said of the clean animals that Noah offered. It was said of his righteousness and his perfection, which he had in his generation. For God does not delight in blood and the smoke of sacrifices, as the demons do. But "since we have been raised with Christ, let us seek the things above," keeping in mind the words "Let my prayer be set before you like incense." As John says in Revelation, "The incense is the prayers of the saints." But if we defile our prayer with wicked thoughts, the words "Let their prayer become sin" come true. The opposite happens if we pray out of righteousness. For those who say because of their sin, "My wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness," the incense becomes foul-smelling. That is why Isaiah said: "If you bring fine flour, it is in vain; incense is an abomination to me." The apostle taught how we ought to pray when he said: "I want the men to pray in every place, lifting up holy hands without anger or arguing." When Moses raised such hands, Israel was winning; when he lowered them, Amalek was winning. Whoever prays like this does not fail, for the saying proves true: "While you are still speaking, he will say, 'Here I am.'" So, he says, the Lord could no longer bear the incense of the wicked. In the same way we may put up with a bad smell for a while, but we flee it when it grows stronger. God, too, has a limit to his forbearance and punishes those who do not repent. He did this in Noah's time, when he could no longer bear the stench of those who were sinning then. That is why he says in the prophets: "I have kept silent; shall I keep silent forever?"

When bodies have rotted, the air around them absorbs the corruption and spreads plague to whoever comes near, and the place becomes impassable. In the same way, the sins of souls produce a plague of souls.

Baruch grieved with the people and lamented, and he pleaded with God on their behalf. So he received a promise of help in his troubles, as God said: "Those I tear down I will build up again." For first "he causes pain, and then he restores," and so on. Good things cannot be received unless the bad ones have first been removed. As the architect of "the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched and not man," he also tears down the wretched buildings of unbelievers. Paul speaks of that true building when he says, "You are God's building." He is also like a farmer who has pulled up what bears no fruit (for "every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted"). He plants a "fruitful vine," not like the vine "turned to bitterness and foreign," which he cuts down so that he may make it "true" again and "God's field." In this way, as David says, he "broke down the hedge" of the vine "brought out of Egypt," and David prays for it: "Look down from heaven and visit this vine." So these people, too, are disciplined for their benefit, for "the Lord disciplines the one he loves." And "who is it that makes me glad, if not the one I have grieved?" For "godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret." That is why I bring evils on all flesh, that is, on those whose minds are set on earthly things.
For God finds the souls of the righteous, since "the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God." The souls of sinners, however, are counted as if they did not even exist.
